home.title: Choose a model
home.subtitle: Pick one, give it data, press Train and watch what it learns. Each card shows the picture you will see inside.

first.title: New to machine learning? Start here.
first.body: A 2-minute guided run: LogisticRegression learns to separate Two moons while you watch the border move. “Recently used” fills up once you’ve trained something.

viz.title: Watch the border move
viz.body: The shade shows how sure the model is. The thick line is where it switches between classes; the dashed one is where it was 10 steps ago.

loss.title: Loss goes down
loss.body: Loss measures how wrong the model is on the training points. Lower is better. When it flattens out, training has converged.

params.title: Change a parameter
params.body: Drag C to 0.01, then to 100. The model retrains instantly — compare how smooth or tight the border becomes.

metric.title: Check it on new data
metric.body: Accuracy is measured on points the model never saw during training. That is the honest score.

linear.title: Linear models
linear.desc: Draw a straight line or a flat border through the data. Fast and easy to read.

trees.title: Trees and ensembles
trees.desc: Ask yes/no questions about features. Ensembles combine many trees into one answer.

other.title: Other classifiers
other.desc: Different ideas of “similar”: margins, neighbours, probabilities, neurons.

unsupervised.title: Unsupervised
unsupervised.desc: No target column. Find groups, or a simpler view of the data.

LinearRegression.desc: Predicts a number as a weighted sum of the features — the line or plane with the smallest squared error.
LinearRegression.when: a first baseline for any number; roughly straight trends
LinearRegression.pro: instant and fully readable: one weight per feature
LinearRegression.con: can't bend to curves; outliers pull it hard

LogisticRegression.desc: Classifies with a straight border: a weighted sum of the features goes through a sigmoid to become a probability.
LogisticRegression.when: a classification baseline; classes split by a line or plane
LogisticRegression.con: only straight borders unless you add features

Ridge.desc: Linear regression with an L2 penalty: big weights cost extra, so all weights shrink towards zero.
Ridge.when: many correlated features, or more features than rows
Ridge.con: keeps every feature — no weight becomes exactly 0

Lasso.desc: Linear regression with an L1 penalty that pushes weak weights to exactly zero, so it also selects features.
Lasso.when: you suspect only a few features matter
Lasso.pro: built-in feature selection, a sparse model
Lasso.con: among correlated features keeps one almost at random

ElasticNet.desc: Linear regression with both L1 and L2 penalties: shrinks every weight and zeroes some; l1_ratio sets the mix.
ElasticNet.when: many features, some correlated, and you want a sparse model

SGDClassifier.desc: A linear classifier trained by stochastic gradient descent: it nudges the weights after every small batch of points.
SGDClassifier.pro: scales to millions of rows, learns online
SGDClassifier.con: sensitive to feature scaling and step size

DecisionTreeClassifier.desc: Asks yes/no questions about one feature at a time (x ≤ threshold?) and answers with the majority class of the leaf it reaches.
DecisionTreeClassifier.when: you need rules a person can read

RandomForestClassifier.desc: Many decision trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample with random feature choices; the forest averages their probabilities.
RandomForestClassifier.when: a strong default for tabular data
RandomForestClassifier.pro: accurate and robust with little tuning
RandomForestClassifier.con: hundreds of trees are hard to explain

ExtraTreesClassifier.desc: A forest whose split thresholds are drawn at random (the best random one is kept); the trees' probabilities are averaged.
ExtraTreesClassifier.when: forest-level accuracy, faster, on noisy data
ExtraTreesClassifier.con: smoother borders can miss sharp edges

GradientBoostingClassifier.desc: Adds shallow trees one by one; each new tree is fitted to the loss gradient, correcting what the ensemble still gets wrong.
GradientBoostingClassifier.when: tabular data where top accuracy matters

HistGradientBoostingClassifier.desc: Gradient boosting that first bins each feature into ≤ 255 buckets, so finding splits is fast; stops early on its own.
HistGradientBoostingClassifier.pro: much faster than classic boosting; handles missing values
HistGradientBoostingClassifier.con: binning loses detail on small data

AdaBoostClassifier.desc: Trains stumps in turn, giving more weight to the points earlier ones got wrong; the final vote is weighted by each stump's accuracy.
AdaBoostClassifier.when: clean data where simple rules add up
AdaBoostClassifier.pro: few parameters, big gain over one stump
AdaBoostClassifier.con: noisy labels get ever more weight

BaggingClassifier.desc: Trains copies of one base model (a tree by default) on bootstrap samples and averages their predictions.
BaggingClassifier.when: an unstable model needs to be steadier
BaggingClassifier.pro: cuts variance without changing the model
BaggingClassifier.con: doesn't fix bias: weak models stay weak

SVC.desc: Finds the border with the widest margin between classes; a kernel lets the border curve, and only the support vectors decide.
SVC.keywords: svm support vector machine margin kernel
SVC.when: small to medium data with complex, clean borders
SVC.pro: strong in high dimensions, flexible kernels

KNeighborsClassifier.desc: Keeps the training points; for a new point it finds the k nearest and takes their (optionally distance-weighted) vote.
KNeighborsClassifier.pro: no training; follows any border shape
KNeighborsClassifier.con: slow predictions on big data; needs scaling

GaussianNB.desc: Models each feature as a bell curve per class, independently; multiplies the likelihoods by the class prior and picks the largest.
GaussianNB.when: very little data or a fast baseline
GaussianNB.pro: trains instantly, works with few rows
GaussianNB.con: the independence assumption makes it overconfident

MLPClassifier.desc: A neural network: layers of neurons take weighted sums through a nonlinearity; backpropagation tunes the weights to cut log-loss.
MLPClassifier.when: curved or complex patterns with enough data
MLPClassifier.con: needs scaling and tuning; a black box

KMeans.desc: Groups points into k clusters: each point joins its nearest center, each center moves to its points' mean, repeated until stable.
KMeans.pro: simple and fast, even on big data
KMeans.con: you choose k; fails on stretched clusters

DBSCAN.desc: Grows clusters from dense areas: a point with enough neighbours within eps is a core; points reachable from cores join, the rest are noise.
DBSCAN.when: clusters of any shape, with outliers
DBSCAN.pro: no cluster count needed; flags noise

PCA.desc: Rotates the data onto new axes ordered by variance and keeps the first few — a linear projection that loses the least spread.
PCA.when: seeing or compressing many correlated features
PCA.con: only linear structure; axes are hard to name

CatBoostClassifier.desc: Gradient boosting on symmetric trees (one question per level); reads categorical columns as text via ordered target statistics.
CatBoostClassifier.con: a large library; slower trees on categories

CatBoostRegressor.desc: CatBoost for numbers: symmetric boosted trees minimise RMSE, and categorical columns are read natively.
CatBoostRegressor.when: predicting numbers from tables with categories
CatBoostRegressor.pro: accurate out of the box, handles categories and gaps
CatBoostRegressor.con: far less readable than a linear model

params.title: Parameters
params.noData: No data yet — pick a preset.

LogisticRegression.C: C is the inverse strength of regularization. Regularization penalizes large weights. Small C = strong penalty: a calm border that single points barely move. Big C = weak penalty: the model tries to get every point right and can overfit. Default 1.0 — try 0.01 and 100 and compare the border.
LogisticRegression.max_iter: Each iteration is one step of the optimizer. Training stops earlier when the border stops moving (converged).
LogisticRegression.class_weight: With 'balanced', mistakes on a rare class cost more, so the model can't just ignore it.

DecisionTreeClassifier.max_depth: Depth = how many questions in a row. Depth 1 is a single cut. Deep trees carve tiny boxes around single points — great on training data, worse on new data.

KMeans.n_clusters: KMeans always returns exactly k groups. Watch the silhouette score: it tells you whether this k splits the data well.

MLPClassifier.hidden_layer_sizes: Each number is one hidden layer and how many neurons it has. More neurons can draw more complex borders but need more data and time.

adv.title: Advanced settings
adv.intro: You rarely need these. Every value has a safe default — change one at a time and watch what the loss does.
adv.splitHint: Which 25% of the rows are held out for testing (stratified by class). Change it to see how much the score depends on the split.

viz.boundaryTip: Every spot of the plane is coloured by the class the model would predict there. The stronger the colour, the surer the model.
viz.treeTip: Read top to bottom: each box asks a yes/no question about one feature. Leaves give the answer. Click a box to see its region.
viz.boundaryNetTip: Left: the border the network draws. Right: the network itself — hover a point to see which neurons fire.
viz.kmeansTip: Each point joins its nearest center; each center moves to the middle of its points. Repeat until nothing moves.
viz.dbscanTip: Dense crowds become clusters. Points with too few neighbours are noise (hollow rings).
viz.pcaTip: The data, turned so the two directions with the most spread become the axes. Arrows show how the original features point.
viz.regLineTip: The line is the model’s prediction for every x. Points are the real values.
viz.regSurfaceTip: Colour = predicted value at that spot. Thin lines join spots with the same prediction.
viz.kmeansNote: No target used — colours are the groups it found, not true classes.
viz.addAs: Click the plot to add a {{cls}} point
viz.shade: Shade = how sure the model is
viz.pathKey: where each center moved, iteration by iteration
viz.pcaPlane: PCA view of {{n}} features · {{p}}% of spread
viz.pcaPlaneTip: More than 2 features: the plane shows the first two principal components. The model still uses all features.
viz.editHint: Click: add · drag: move · Alt+click: delete

plot.aria: Plot of {{x}} and {{y}}. Arrow keys pan, + and − zoom, 0 resets.

needs_features.title: There are no feature columns
needs_features.body: Every column is the target. Add at least one column the model can learn from.

missing_values.title: The data has empty cells
missing_values.body: Column {{column}} has {{count}} empty cell(s). Models can’t train on empty cells.

too_few_rows.title: Too few rows to learn from
too_few_rows.body: There are only {{rows}} rows. Use at least 10 so there is something to learn and something to test on.

needs_two_features.title: PCA needs at least two features
needs_two_features.body: With one feature there is nothing to squeeze. Load data with more columns.

no_target.title: No target column
no_target.body: {{model}} learns to predict a column. Pick which column is the target.

needs_category_target.title: {{model}} predicts categories, but your target is a number
needs_category_target.body: The target column {{target}} holds numbers like 7.3. A classifier needs labels from a fixed list.

needs_numeric_target.title: {{model}} predicts numbers, but your target is a category
needs_numeric_target.body: The target column {{target}} holds labels — {{values}}. Linear regression can only output a number like 7.3, so it can’t learn labels.

one_class.title: Only one class in the target
one_class.body: Every row has the same label, so there is nothing to tell apart.

too_many_classes.title: Too many classes ({{count}})
too_many_classes.body: Sightline shows up to {{max}} classes so every one keeps its own colour and shape.

class_too_small.title: Class {{cls}} has a single row
class_too_small.body: Each class needs at least two rows so one can go to the test set.

switch_model.text: Switch to {{model}} — made for this kind of target.

change_target.text: Change the target — pick a column that fits{{column}}.

edit_table.text: Fix the table — fill or drop the problem cells.

ctl.noPause: Nothing to pause: fitted in one go
ctl.noPauseTree: Nothing to pause: a tree is built in one pass
ctl.noStep: Nothing to step: fitted in one go
ctl.stepTree: Replay the growth one level at a time

loss.lossTip: Loss measures how wrong the model is: 0 would be perfect. Solid = training points, dashed = test points. If the dashed line rises while the solid one falls, the model starts to memorise noise.
loss.inertiaHint: total squared distance from points to their center · lower = tighter groups
loss.inertiaTip: KMeans has no loss. Inertia = total squared distance from points to their center; it only goes down.
loss.boostTip: Each stage adds one small tree. When validation stops improving, more trees only memorise noise.
loss.treesTip: Trees are trained independently, so there is no loss to follow. The curve shows the forest getting steadier as it grows.
loss.depthTip: A tree is built in a single pass. The bars replay how accuracy changed as the tree grew deeper.
loss.onestepTip: Fitted with one call — nothing to animate. Shows what was learned instead of a curve.
loss.onestepRegTip: Solved with one formula — no iterations. Errors bunched around 0 mean a good fit; a lopsided shape means a missed pattern.
loss.knnTip: KNN just stores the training points. Instead of a loss, see how the number of neighbours changes the score.
loss.pcaTip: PCA has no loss. Each bar is the share of the data’s spread one component holds.
loss.pcaText: The {{n}} kept components hold {{p}}% of the data’s spread.
loss.doneIn: Done in {{ms}} ms — nothing to animate
loss.treeText: A tree has no training curve: it is built in a single pass, so there is no loss falling over time. The chart shows how accuracy changed as the tree grew deeper.
loss.treeReplay: Press +1 level to replay the growth.
loss.svcText: {{sv}} of {{n}} training points became support vectors — only they shape the border.
loss.svcRing: Ringed points on the plot are the support vectors.
loss.dbText: Found {{c}} clusters, {{noise}} noise points, {{core}} core points.

metric.accuracyTip: the share of test points the model labels correctly. 0.87 means 87 of every 100. Test points were hidden during training, so this is how the model does on new data.
metric.r2Tip: how much of the target’s variation the model explains. 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than always guessing the average. Measured on test points.
metric.silhouetteTip: how well each point sits in its own group compared with the nearest other group. From −1 (wrong group) to 1 (clearly separated). Above 0.5 is a good split.
metric.varianceTip: the share of the data’s spread the kept components still hold. 1.0 = nothing lost.

net.title: Network
net.tip: Columns are layers. Lines are weights: solid accent = positive, dashed = negative, thicker = bigger. Fill = how strongly a neuron fires for the hovered point.
net.empty: The network appears after the first epoch.
net.fill: fill = how strongly a neuron fires for point #{{id}}
net.hoverHint: hover a point to see which neurons fire

regions.title: Regions it carved
regions.tip: Every leaf owns a box of the plane. Select a node in the tree to outline its box.
regions.cut: Every split is a straight cut parallel to an axis.

data.title: Get data
data.presetsHint: One click to a ready-made shape. Tweak the 2–3 settings that matter, then use it.

table.missing: {{count}} empty cell(s) in {{col}} (row {{rows}}). Models can’t train on empty cells.
table.name: Name
table.typeHint: Numeric = numbers you can compare (weight). Category = labels from a fixed list (colour).
table.numbersHint: Use “Numbers” for codes like 1, 2, 3 that are labels, not amounts.
table.oneHot: Text categories are turned into numbers automatically (one-hot) before training.
table.targetHint: The target is what the model learns to predict. Only one column can be the target — now it is {{name}}.
table.noTarget: No target yet: the table can be used by KMeans, DBSCAN and PCA.
table.readyFor: What this table is ready for
table.readyClassHint: Works with all 13 classifiers. The 4 regression models need a numeric target; KMeans, DBSCAN and PCA ignore the target.
table.readyRegHint: Works with the 4 regression models. Classifiers need a category target.

gen.fillHint: Random fills every column with noise. Rules let you set a range, a distribution or a list of values for each one.
gen.normalHint: Bell shape: most values near the mean, few far away.
gen.uniformHint: Flat: every value in the range is equally likely.
gen.ruleCircle: B if inside the circle around ({{a}}, {{b}}), else A
gen.ruleXor: B if {{a}} and {{b}} have the same sign, else A
gen.noise: Noise level · labels flipped at random
gen.noiseHint: 0% = a perfectly clean border. More noise makes the task harder and more realistic.
gen.dashed: dashed = the rule’s border · points on the wrong side = noise

ins.statsTip: mean = typical value · std = typical distance from the mean · min / max = the extremes.
ins.statsHint: mean = typical value · std = how far values usually sit from the mean
ins.balanceTip: How many rows each class has.
ins.balanceHint: If one class were much smaller, accuracy could look good while the model ignores it. Then try class_weight='balanced'.
ins.outliersTip: A value is an outlier when it lies more than 1.5 × IQR below the first quartile or above the third.
ins.outliersHint: Points more than 1.5 × IQR outside the middle half of a feature.
ins.pairAbout: How to read a pair plot
ins.pairTip: Each cell plots one feature against another. Hover a point to find it in every cell.
ins.pairHint: Diagonal: how each feature is spread (histogram, stacked by class). Off-diagonal: every pair of features plotted against each other.
ins.boxAbout: How to read a box plot
ins.boxTip: The box covers the middle half of the values; the line inside is the median; whiskers reach the furthest normal values.
ins.sameScale: Same scale for every row: {{lo}} to {{hi}}.
ins.spreadText: {{wide}} spreads about {{r}}× wider than {{narrow}}. Models that measure distance (KNN, SVC) and neural networks can over-weight the wider feature.
ins.scaleHint: Uses StandardScaler: every feature gets mean 0 and std 1. Trees don’t need it.
ins.corrHint: −1 … 1. Near 0: knowing one feature tells you little about the other.

decide.title: How it decides
decide.clickHint: or click any point on the plot
decide.trainFirstBody: Then pick any point and follow the model’s reasoning step by step.
decide.incorrect: The prediction is wrong for this point.
decide.barsHint: Orange bars push toward {{b}}, blue bars toward {{a}}.
decide.sigTitle: Sigmoid: turn z into a probability
decide.signTitle: Sign: which side of the border

1.title: Read the features
1.detail: The model only sees these numbers{{scaled}}. It knows nothing else about the point.

2.title: Multiply by the weights
2.detail: During training the model learned {{ws}}. A big weight means that feature matters a lot.

3.title: Add them up
3.detail: Add the products and the intercept. z above 0 means “{{b}} side of the border”, below 0 means “{{a}} side”. Here z = {{z}}.

5.title: Pick the class
5.detail: If P({{b}}) is at least 0.5 the answer is {{b}}, otherwise {{a}}. The model says {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

4.title: Squash with the sigmoid
4.detail: The sigmoid bends any number into a probability between 0 and 1. z = 0 becomes 0.5; the further z is from 0, the surer the model. z = {{z}} gives P({{b}}) = {{prob}}.

4.title: Look at the sign of z
4.detail: With the {{loss}} loss there is no probability: only the side of the border counts. Positive z → {{b}}, negative → {{a}}.

1.title: Read the features
1.detail: SGDClassifier draws a straight border like logistic regression. It only sees these numbers{{scaled}}.

2.title: Multiply by the weights
2.detail: The weights were learned a few samples at a time: {{ws}}.

3.title: Add them up
3.detail: z is the signed distance-like score to the border. Here z = {{z}}.

1.title: Read the features
1.detail: The model only sees these numbers. With {{k}} classes it keeps one set of weights per class.

2.title: One score per class
2.detail: Each class multiplies the features by its own weights and adds its intercept.

3.title: Softmax
3.detail: Softmax turns the scores into probabilities that sum to 1. Bigger score → bigger share.

4.title: Pick the class
4.detail: The class with the biggest probability wins: {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

3.title: Compare the scores
3.detail: One-vs-rest: each class has its own border; the class with the highest score wins.

1.title: Read the features
1.detail: The model only sees these numbers.

2.title: Multiply by the weights
2.detail: Each weight says how much the prediction changes when that feature grows by 1.

3.title: Add the intercept
3.detail: The sum is the prediction — there is no squashing for regression.

4.title: Compare with the truth
4.detail: The error (real − predicted) is what training tried to make small, on average, across all points.

1.title: Start at the root
1.detail: The root asks the most useful first question: {{q}}? It was picked because no other single cut separates the classes better.

2.title: Answer: {{q}}?
2.detail: {{f}} = {{v}} is not above the threshold, so the point follows the “yes” branch. {{n}} training points reached this node.

3.title: Answer: {{q}}?
3.detail: {{f}} = {{v}} is above the threshold, so the point follows the “no” branch. {{n}} training points reached this node.

4.title: Read the leaf
4.detail: A leaf doesn’t calculate anything. It reports the majority class of the training points that ended up in it ({{mix}}) — {{verdict}}

1.title: Locate the point
1.detail: KMeans has no labels to learn from. It only knows where this point is and where the {{k}} centers ended up after {{rounds}} rounds of training.

2.title: Measure distances
2.detail: It measures the ordinary straight-line distance from the point to each of the {{k}} centers — the dashed lines.

3.title: Pick the nearest center
3.detail: Smallest distance wins. Center {{best}} is {{bd}} away; the runner-up, center {{second}}, is {{sd}} away — {{clear}}

4.title: Join that group
4.detail: The point takes group {{best}}’s colour and shape. There is no probability here: KMeans gives a hard yes/no assignment.

km.h1: Every point joins its nearest center — exactly what you see on the left.
km.h2: Each center moves to the average position of its points.
km.h3: Repeat until the centers stop moving. Here that took {{n}} rounds.

1.title: Feed in the features
1.detail: The input neurons simply hold the point’s feature values.

2.title: Hidden layer {{l}}
2.detail: Each neuron multiplies its inputs by its own weights, adds a bias, then applies {{act}}. {{next}}

3.title: Output neuron
3.detail: The output layer ({{oa}}) turns the last hidden layer into class probabilities.

mlp.first: Each neuron reacts to one direction in the plane.
mlp.deeper: Combining several straight cuts is how the network draws curved borders.
mlp.legend: thicker = bigger weight · fill = how strongly the neuron fires · dashed ring = output 0
mlp.m1a: no maths yet — the inputs are just the feature values
mlp.m1n: The network only sees these numbers.
mlp.reluNote: relu keeps positive sums and turns negative ones into 0.
mlp.outNote: One output neuron is enough for two classes; more classes use softmax.

1.title: Send the point down every tree
1.detail: Each tree was trained on a random slice of the data, so they disagree a little.

2.title: Each tree answers
2.detail: Every tree gives its own probability for each class.

3.title: Average the answers
3.detail: A soft vote: the probabilities are averaged, which smooths out single trees’ mistakes.

4.title: Highest average wins
4.detail: The class with the highest average wins: {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

forest.showing: Showing {{k}} of {{n}}. Each number is that tree’s P({{cls}}).

1.title: Start from the base guess
1.detail: Before any tree, the guess comes from the class shares in the training data.

2.title: Each small tree adds a correction
2.detail: Every tree was trained on the mistakes left by the trees before it, so each nudges the score.

3.title: Add everything up
3.detail: The corrections add up into one raw score.

4.title: Squash the score
4.detail: The sigmoid turns the score into a probability: {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

boost.title: Corrections add up
boost.hint: Orange pushes toward the second class, blue toward the first.

4.title: Softmax over the scores
4.detail: Each class has its own score; softmax turns them into probabilities. {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

1.title: Each model votes
1.detail: Each weak tree votes for one class. Its say grows with how accurate it was during training.

2.title: Weigh the votes
2.detail: The votes are added up, weighted by each model’s say.

3.title: Biggest share wins
3.detail: The class with the biggest weighted share wins: {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

ada.title: Strongest {{n}} voters
ada.hint: Bar = the model’s say (weight). Colour = the class it votes for.

1.title: Measure the distance to every training point
1.detail: KNN stores the training points and measures how far each one is from this point.{{self}}

2.title: Keep the {{k}} closest
2.detail: Only the k nearest neighbours matter; everything else is ignored.

3.title: They vote
3.detail: Each neighbour votes for its class{{weighted}}.

knn.self: This is a training point, so its nearest neighbour is itself.

1.title: Compare with each support vector
1.detail: Only the support vectors — points on or inside the margin — shape the border. The kernel ({{kernel}}) measures how similar the point is to each.

2.title: Weighted sum = signed distance
2.detail: Each support vector pulls toward its class, weighted by what it learned. The sum is the decision value.

3.title: The sign picks the side
3.detail: Positive → one side of the border, negative → the other: {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

2.title: One score per class
2.detail: With more classes, each class gets its own decision score.

1.title: Start from the class shares
1.detail: Before looking at the point, each class is as likely as it was in the training data.

2.title: How typical is each feature?
2.detail: For each class, a bell curve per feature says how typical this value is. Features are treated separately — that’s the “naive” part.

3.title: Multiply
3.detail: Multiply the prior by every feature’s likelihood, separately for each class.

4.title: Rescale to sum to 1
4.detail: Dividing by the total gives probabilities. {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

nb.normalize: Multiply, then rescale to sum to 1

1.title: Draw a circle of radius eps
1.detail: DBSCAN looks at the neighbourhood of radius eps around the point.

2.title: Count the points inside
2.detail: The point needs at least {{ms}} points within eps to be a dense core point.

3.title: Core, border or noise?
3.detail: Enough neighbours → core. Fewer, but next to a core point → border. Neither → noise.

4.title: Join the cluster it touches
4.detail: Core and border points join the cluster of the core points they connect to.

5.title: Marked as noise
5.detail: Too few neighbours and no core point nearby: DBSCAN leaves it out of every cluster.

db.coreText: It has enough neighbours within eps, so it anchors a cluster.
db.borderText: Not dense enough itself, but within eps of a core point.
db.noiseText: Not dense enough and no core point within eps.
db.noCircle: ringed = neighbours within eps (measured in model space)
db.trainingOnly: DBSCAN has no predict(): these steps explain training points only.

1.title: Center the point
1.detail: PCA first moves the data so its average sits at 0.{{whiten}}

2.title: Project onto component 1
2.detail: A dot product with the first component — the direction with the most spread.

3.title: Project onto component 2
3.detail: A second dot product gives the vertical position on the plot.

pca.whiten: With whiten on, each score is then divided by that component’s spread.

1.title: Take the row as it is
1.detail: CatBoost reads categories as text ({{cats}}); it turns each category into a number itself (a target statistic computed in a random order), so nothing is one-hot encoded.

2.title: Tree 1: one question per level
2.detail: CatBoost trees are symmetric: every node on a level asks the same question, so {{depth}} answers pick one of {{leaves}} leaves. This leaf adds {{lv}}.

3.title: Add up all {{n}} trees
3.detail: Each tree was fitted to what the trees before it still got wrong; their leaf values, each shrunk by the learning rate {{lr}}, add up to the raw score, starting from {{base}}.

4.title: Turn the score into a probability
4.detail: The sigmoid maps the score to the probability of the second class: {{pick}} — {{verdict}}

cat.rowHint: Categories go in as text — no one-hot columns.
cat.rowHintNoCats: This dataset has only numbers; with a text column CatBoost would read it directly.
cat.treeHint: Same question across a whole level: that is what makes CatBoost trees fast and hard to overfit.

4.title: Pick the highest probability
4.detail: Each class has its own score; softmax turns them into probabilities that sum to 1. {{pick}} wins — {{verdict}}

4.title: The score is the prediction
4.detail: For regression the raw score is the answer: {{y}}. The true value is {{truth}} (error {{err}}).

cb.catTag: cat_features: {{cols}} — read as text, no one-hot
cb.catTip: CatBoost gets {{cols}} as categories (cat_features) and turns each value into a target statistic itself. The other models in Sightline see these columns one-hot encoded.
cb.noCats: No categorical columns — add an “Aa” column in the generator to see CatBoost's native categories
cb.noCatsTip: CatBoost's strength is categorical data: Data → Generator → switch a column to Aa, or import a CSV with text columns.
